Kalukhasia muLuyia:
1. I see a child.
2. I am able to cook well.
3. You (sing.) are helping the old lady.
4. You (pl.) are counting the people.
5. Where do you live?
6. I am a girl.
7. You are a woman.
8. I cook now.
9. We ask the people.
10. The boys see the children.
11. The old women are talking together.
12. You (sing.) are able to help the old women well.
13. The children do badly.
14. This person asks that boy.
15. That woman helps that woman yonder.
16. These people are able to talk together.
17. That lady helps that old woman yonder.
18. That child yonder asks those yonder.
19. Those friends yonder are able to cook together with those (people).
20. A person is able to do well, or he is able to do badly.
21. Those ladies live well.
22. You live here, don't you?
23. The boys are present, aren't they?
24. Where are the boys?
25. The girl helps the old woman a little now.
26. How are you?
27. How are the girls?
28. How are the boys doing?
29. How are the boys doing?
30. That person does evil.

The Habitual or Continuous Forms of Verbs
In English, when we are in the act of cooking, we say, "I am cooking." This may be expressed in Luyia in two ways. (1) S P + V R + a = endekhanya; (2) S P + V R + anga = endekhanya.

When we say, "I cook every week," we use the simple verb stem. Luyia uses the habitual or continuous endings as follows.
1. verbs ending in -a, V R + anga.
2. verbs ending in -ia, V R + nija.
3. verbs ending in -ia (this verb root includes the i).
4. verbs ending in -ie, V R + njie.
5. verbs ending in -et, V R + enje.

The continuous root ending is -ng, and like vowels must precede and follow it. If those vowels are i or e, palatalization takes place, changing -ng- to -nj-. See the Palatalization rules in the Introduction.

Some verbs have the idea of entering into a state. While entering into this state, the continuous ending is used. Once the state is entered into, the past tense is used. Menya is sometimes used in this sense, thus using its past tense stem menyile. Omenyile heena? - "Where do you live?" or, "Where have you entered into the state of living?" Other verbs are in this idea group.
- chinga - carry uses chinjile.
- sinjila - stand uses sinjile.
- ikhala - sit uses ikhaale.
The S P for he/she of these three verb forms is u.

The following is menya in the continuous form.
Singular Plural
1st Per. emenyanga - I live khumenyanga - we are living
2nd Per. omenyanga - you live mumenyanga - you are living
3rd Per. amenyanga - he/she lives bamenyanga - they are living

5. What is the boy doing?

Negative Construction
There are two negative forms in Luyia, the shi...ta/tawe and the ra...ta/tawe forms. The shi...tawe form is used for the indicative mood, i.e. a statement of fact.
Pattern: shi + S P + V R + ending + ta or tawe.
When the shi comes before the S P an-, for "I," the a of the en drops out. When the n of the prefix is elided before certain other consonants, there is no subject prefix. The entire en is elided. For compensation there is a lengthening of the i of shi in pronunciation.
Shindeekhama tawe. I do not cook.
Shikhoonya omushie ta. I am not helping the old woman.
Shiabala abandu ta. She is not counting the people.
Exercise 7
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1. Omnyile hano, nohomba? Shimenyile hano ta. 2. Omukhasi shiateekhange bulaano ta. 3. Abandu yabo shibaboolelans halala ta. 4. Omusiani uno shibaboolelansang nomusiani ywo tawe. 5. Omukhaama ulia shianyala okhuteekha bulayi ta. 6. Shionyala okhukhoorya bulaano ta. 7. Abaana bano shibreebe yabo ta. 8. Shiboolela omukhaama yuu okhukhoorya omushie ulia ta. 9. Oteekhanga bulaano, noho? Shimdeekha bulaano ta. 10. Muli abekhasi? Shikhuli abakhasi ta/khuli absama.
Exercise 8
Kalukhasia muLuyia:
1. You (s.) live here, don't you? (No,) I do not live here. 2. The woman is not cooking now. 3. Those people are not talking together. 4. This boy is not talking with that boy. 5. That girl yonder is not able to cook well. 6. You (s.) are not able to help now. 7. These children do not ask those. 8. You (s.) are not telling this girl to help that old woman yonder. 9. You (s.) are cooking now, aren't you? (No,) I am not cooking now. 10. Are you women? (No,) we are not women; we are children.
Giving Commands
There are two ways of giving commands in Luyia.
1. The imperative mood is the more authoritative.
Singular Plural
Patterns: Verbs ending in -at, V R + a/ange VR + e/enje
Verbs ending in -ta, V R + ia/inja VR + ie/injie
Vowel stem verbs: y + VR + a/ange y + VR + e/enje
y + VR + ie/injie y + VR + ie/injie
When i or e follows k, kh, or ng, they change them to ch,sh, and nh.
Imperatives may be interjections in Luyia.
Verb Meaning Singular Plural (all of you)
teekha cook teekha/teekhange - cook teesha/teesheheje
tola see tola/tolanga - see lole/lolenje
langa call langa/langanga - call lanje/lanjerje
kasia fix, make kasia/kasinja - fix kasie/kasinje
eva sweep eva/evanya - sweep,dust yevo/yevenje
osia wash osia/osinja - wash yosie/yosinje
ska study ska/ska - study yeche/yechenje

Lanje omukhaama ulia. 12. Boola hatiti. 13. Rebe abandu. 14. Kasinja ingo. 15. Yosinja omwana. 16. Yeye hano. 17. Yosia bulayi. 18. Langa abagizi. 19. Yeka bulayi. 20. Yeche bulaano.

Exercise 10
Kalukhasia muLuluyia: (Use both singular and plural forms.)
1. Cook now. 2. Work here. 3. Sweep well. 4. Look! 5. Count the children. 6. Cook well. 7. Call the child. 8. Live well. 9. Help that woman. 10. Talk together now. 11. Call that girl yonder. 12. Speak a little. 13. Ask the people. 14. Be fixing the home. 15. Be washing the child. 16. Sweep here. 17. Wash well. 18. Call the children. 19. Study well. 20. Study now.
2. The subjunctive mood is the gentle, polite form.
Several uses of the subjunctive mood are related to commands.
a. In giving instructions, and asking specific instructions.
"She is to cook now." "May I help?" "Let them speak," etc.
b. Expressing wishes and desires.
"May you live well," "May they work well," etc.
c. All commands may be given in the subjunctive mood, or the first may be in the imperative and the following ones in the subjunctive. Tsia olole omwana - "Go and see the child."
d. In asking and giving permission.
Endeeshe bulaano? - "May I cook now?"
Da, cheeshe balaano. - "Yes, you may cook now."
Pattern for the subjunctive: SP + VR + e/enje. Use ba for verb "to be."
Singular
1st Per. endeeshe - let me cook; shall I cook? may I cook? am I to cook?
2nd Per. oteeshe - cook; you may cook/are to cook; may you cook.
3rd Per. aeeshe - he/she may/is to cook; let her/may she cook.
Plural
1st Per. khuteshenje - let us cook; may we cook? we are to cook.
2nd Per. mutesee - cook; you may/are to cook; may you cook.
3rd Per. bateshenje - they may/are to be cooking; may they/let them
Exercise 11
Kalukhasia mulugungi: (Translate in all possible ways.)
1. Emboolie bulaano. 2. Ee, obole bulaano. 3. Olole omwana. 4. Mukhoo-nye abukhasi. 5. Omenyengeje bulayi. 6. Mukholemje bulayi. 7. Orreeb omwana. 8. Maboolelane bulaano. 9. Obolele omukhasi ateeshes bulaano. 10. Okoonreye bulayi. 11. Omsianii abale bulayi. 12. Boolela omsianii abale bulayi. 13. Abakhasana bateeshe bulaano, ncho? Ee, batoeshe bulaano. 14. Khube heena? Mube hano. 15. Abasana babe halina. 16. Obeho.
Exercise 12
Kalukhasia muLuluyia: (Do in all possible ways, singular and plural.)
1. May I/am to speak now? Yes, you may/are to speak now. 2. See the child. 3. Help the women. 4. Always live well. 5. Work well; may you always work well. 6. Ask the child; you may ask the child. 7. Speak together now; you may speak together now. 8. Tell the woman to cook now/she may cook now/she is to cook now. 9. May you/you are to . Help well. 10. May/let the boy count well. 11. Tell the boy to count well. 12. May/are the girls to cook now? Yes, they may/are to cook now. 13. May I be a lady. 14. Where may we be/are we to be? You may/are to be here. 15. Let the children be over yonder; the children may/are to be over yonder. 16. Goodbye (lit. may you remain/be here. The verb "to be" is used for "be" and "remain.")
Negative Commands
These are always in the negative subjunctive. The ra...tawe/taw negative is used.
Pattern: SP + re + VR + a/anga or e/ŋia + ta/taw.
Singular
1st per. erateekha tawe - may I/let me not cook; am I not to cook?
2nd per. orateekha ta - you are not to/may not cook
3rd per. arateekha ta - she is not to/may not cook
Plural
1st per. khurateekha ta - we are not to/may not/let us not cook
2nd per. murateekha ta - you are not to/may not cook
3rd per. barateekha ta - they are not to/may not/let them not cook

CHAPTER 2
Vocabulary
heellesia, haana - give
sinjila - stand
yinjila, tive - work
lwala - be sick/ill
lila - cry
mwenya - smile
tselka - laugh
okhuba na-/nende - to
li na-/nende - have,
ni- - am, are, is
shichila - because
mbushinga - why?
okhushila muno - very
much, very
leelo - today
toto - truly, surely
khaaotsi - always,
repeatedly
mbu - that, so that,
in order that
omufundi - skilled
workman
abafundi - skilled
workmen
omukholi, omutiyi - workman
abakholi, abatiyi - workmen
omulwale - sick person, patient
abelwale - sick people, patients
omulami - well person
abalamu - well people
banga? - how many?
abanji - many, too
many
(olundi - certain one, other one
(abandi - some,
others
butinyu - difficult,
hard
butswa - just, free,
nothing
shinga mbu - like
e- - at (a place)
balala - some
wa- - of (sing.)
ba- - of (pl.)
-khwo - some, any,
a little, ever
khandi - and, also,
again
ne - and, but
rebustuma - but
mulale - one (person)
babili - two (people)
batari - three
bene - four
barasano - five
basasa - six
musafu (bane nabate) - seven
mumane - eight
shienda (barano na- bane) - nine
ekhumu, (el)ikhumi - ten
likhumu namulala - eleven
likhumu nababili - twelve
amakhumi kabili - twenty
Oundi and abandi drop their initial vowels when they follow nouns.
omundu undi - a certain one, another one/person
abaana bano nende abandi - these children and the others
In comparing or contrasting two groups of people or two people
one may use milala - "one" or balala - "some" first, the next one
being oundi or abandi. Or abandi .......abandi may be used.
omundu mulala noundi uyo - one person and that other one
Belala batsekha, ne abandi baliila. - Some laugh and others cry.
Abandi batsekha, ne abandi baliila. - Some laugh and others cry.
Ne is a conjunctive between clauses having a sequence of thought.
In speaking the e is elided before another vowel, not in writing.
Mulala atsekha, ne oundi amwenye. - One laughs, and the other
smiles,
Bano batsekhangana, ne yabo balillanga. - These are laughing,
and/but those are crying.
Khandi has many uses.
1. Joins adjectives describing the same noun or pronoun.
Omundi shianyala okhuba omulwale khandi omulamu ta. - A
person cannot be sick and well.
2. Joins adverbs describing the same verb.
Bakholaange bulayi khandi butinyu. - They are working well
and hard.
3. Joins two or more independent clauses having no definite time
sequence but which are parallel in structure. They may be
two or more clauses about the same subject,
Ateekha khandi akhoonya abakhasi. - She is cooking, and
she is helping the women.
or, there may be two or more subjects doing the same thing.
Abakhaha babalanga, khandi abasiani babalanga. - The
girls are counting and the boys are counting.
khwo is a suffix and joins the word it modifies. With positive
construction it can mean "ever," and with negative construction,
"never." It also means "a little," "some," "any," or even "once."
alwalakhwo. - He is a bit sick.
Endikho bulayi. - I am fairly well.
Yabo bateekhkwwo. - Do those ever cook/cook a little/any?
Shibateekhkwwo ta. - They never cook/do not cook any/at all.

Exercise 1
Kalukhasia mulisungu:
1.Omukholi milala, noundi uyo bekholanga bulayi. 2.Abafundi bano
bahili nabandi yabo batamu bekholange butinyu. 3.Omilwale uyu noundi
uyo balikw ho bulayi leelo. 4.Abukholi bano banie nabandi yabo
barana shibayinzilangakhwo leelo ta. 5.Balala belala bayinzilanga,
ne abandi betsekhang'ho. 6.Balala balifinde, ne abandi balala
. 7.Malak ali haro, ne abandi beli halia. 8.Balala baholange
haro, na abandi basinzilange haro khasotso. 9.Bano
bayinzilange bulayi, khandi butinyu, khandi abandi yabe bayinzilanga
bulayi khandi butinyu. 10.Omware uno usinjiile (see p. 3),
khami uyo usinjiile. 11.Otsekhang'khw?. Shiznekhakwokhw to.
12.Abana bano bellang'ahokhshila, ne abandi yabo balilangakhwo.

Exercise 2
Kalukhasia mulisuluya:
1.Ome workman and that other one are doing well. 2.These two fundis
(skilled workmen) and those three others are working hard. 3.This
patient and that other one are better today (are a bit well today).
4.These four workmen and those other five are not working any/at
all today. 5.Some of those yonder are working and the others laugh.
6.Some are crying, but others are sick. 7.One is here, but the
others are yonder. 8.Always some are working here, and the others
are standing here. 9.These are working well and hard, and these
others are working well and hard. 10.This child is standing, and
that one is standing. 11.Do you ever laugh? (No,) I never laugh
at all. 12.These children are crying very much, and those others
are crying a little.

Ni Copula
In the last lesson we noticed the verb stems li and ba - "to be,"
and made sentences with them. But there is a shorter way to say
some of the same things. That is by using the Ni-Copula. It is
used for identification and, when used this way, is preferred to
the full li verb. The i of ni- drops out before another vowel.
Ni- is always joined to the following word unless emphasis is
desired. The tone does not rise where the i is elided.
NiPetero. - It is Peter.
Notiено. - It is Otieno.
Uno nomukhasi. - This is a woman.

To express location the full verb "to be" must be used, also in
negative construction.
Omulina ali heena? Ali haro. - Where is the friend? He is here.
Omwani alino? Shialino tawe. - Is the child here? He is not here.
For now, the ni- copula may be used only with the third person.

Exercise 3
Kalukhasia mulisungu:
1.Omundi uyo nomusasata. 2.Nomwana. 3.Niwina? NiYohana. 4.Nibeema
? Nabawale. 5.Omusani pomolami. 6.Omundi ulia niwina? Nomufundi
. 7.Nabana benga? Melikhumi. (Long ago "ten" was elikhumi.
So the i of ni- drops out before the a.) 8.Balino abanj'i, noho?
9.Omundi uli heena? Ali ingo. 10.Oli omulamau? Tawe, shindi omulamu
tawe.

Exercise 4
Kalukhasia mulisuluya in all possible ways:
1.That person is a man. 2.It is a child. 3.Who is it? It is John.
4.Who are they? They are the sick ones. 5.The boy is well. 6.Who
is that person yonder? He is a fundi (skilled workman). 7.How
many children are they? They are ten. 8.There are many here, aren't
there? 9.Where is the man? He is at home. 10.Are you well?
No, I am not well.

To Have
"To have" is expressed by the verb "to be" + na- or nende. It
means "to be with," and does not have the idea of possession. The
na- coalesces short except with demonstratives beginning with a-e,
and is spoken on a high tone.
Patterns: SP + li + na-/nende; SP + beetsaana + na-/nende; okhuba +
na-/nende; Subjunctive Pattern: SP + be/beetsenje + na-/nende.

1.Endi nende omwana. 2.Embe nende omwana uno? 3.Oli nomukhaana?
Re, endi nende omukhaana. 4.Olikhwo nabalami, neno? Be, Nibanga. 5.Embe nabalami bangas? Obe nabalili. 6.Oli nomusasataa? 7.Ali nende abesaliani? Tawe, ali natakhaana. 8.Omukhasi ali nende abalami musafu. 9.Malikhwo nabalwale hano? Be, Nibanga? Nekhumi. 10.Mibe nende abalina abanj.
Exercise 6
Kalukhasia mululuya: (using all possible ways)
1.I have a child. 2.May I be with this child? 3.Have you a daughter? Yes, I have a daughter. 4.Do you have any children? Yes. How many? They are four. 5.How many children may I be with? You are to be with two. 6.Do you have a husband, are you with a man? 7.Does he have sons? No, he has daughters. 8.The woman has seven children. 9.Do you have any sick people here? Yes. How many? They are ten. 10.May you (pl.) have many friends.
Monosyllabic Verbs
There are three types of verbs in Luyia, monosyllabic, dissyllabic, and polysyllabic. There are two groups of monosyllabic verbs. One group is called (a), and the other group (b). The continuous endings for these are -itsanga for the indicative and negative subjunctive, and -itsenje for the subjunctive positive.
Group (a) uses the verb stem (VS), the final a coalescing long with the ą of -itsanga or -itsenje.
Group (b) uses the verb root with the continuous endings.
Patterns for continuous endings:
Group (a) Indicative
Positive: SP + VS + itsanga
Negative: Shi + SP + VS + itsanga + ta/tawe
Subjunctive
Positive: SP + VS + itsenje +
Negative: SP + ra + VS + itsanga + ta/tawe
Group (b) Indicative
Positive: SP + VR + itsanga
Negative: Shi + SP + VR + itsanga + ta/tawe
Subjunctive
Positive: SP + VR + itsenje
Negative: SP + ra + VR + itsanga + ta/tawe
A complete list of monosyllabic verbs with continuous endings:
Stem Meaning Habitual Indicative Subjunctive Positive
(a) shia - get light shieetsanga shieetsenje
sia(sa) - grind sieetsanga(seetsanga) sieetsenje(seetsenje)
nia - defecate nieetsanga nieetsenje
ba - be, mean beetsanga beetsenje
ha - give (to) heetsanga heetsenje
hwa - come to end hweetsanga hweetsenje
khwa - pay dowry (for) khweetsanga khweetsenje
nywa - drink nyweetsanga nyweetsenje
re - put, place reetsanga reetsenje
(b) fwa - die, faint fritsanga fritsenje
kwe - fall, become kwitsanga kwitsenje
toia - go tsitsanga tsitsenje
via - eat litsanga litsenje
yia - fear, respect fittsanga fittsenje
yia - got hot/done (his) yittsanga yittsenje

1.I am a fundi. 2.Those boys are paying dowry for girls. 3.The children are drinking very much today. 4.Let us (always) put the patients here. 5.Let the girls grind at home; they may not grind here. 6.This person is always ill. 7.Let us always eat at Ekhomo. 8.We are going to Kisumu now. 9.The children fear/respect that man. 10.Where do the fundis eat? 11.Why are many people dying? Because they are very ill. 12.May the man always drink well; may he never drink badly.
Possessive Particles
Possessive particles express "of," such as "a glass of water," "a member of the council," "the child of the man (the man's child)."
The possessive particle is always prefixed to the following word; and forms short coalescence with a following noun, adjective, adverb, or infinitive. The coalesced vowel is spoken on a high tone.
The possessive particles for persons are wa- = "of" for singular, and ba- = "of" for plural. If the preceding noun is singular, wa- is used; if it is plural, ba- is used. The possessive normally follows the noun it modifies unless there is danger of ambiguity.
When the possessive particle is prefixed to a capitalized word, short coalescence takes place. If the capital letter is a vowel, and the capital comes at its usual place.
omwana womukhasi - the child of the woman/the woman's child abalina bomukhasi - the friends of the girl/the girl's friends omwana waDobi - the child of Dobi/Dobi's child omukhasi wOtieno - the wife of Otieno/Otieno's wife omundu wahano - a person of this place/a local person Uno nomundu wokhukhooroya - This is the person to help (of to help)
The vowel ō comes into play for coalescence with nouns beginning with mu-, -m-, -khu-, and khw-.
omundu wokwihila - a Mwihila person omundu wokhumeesa - the person (of) at the table
When the place prefix e- = "at" is used, the possessive particle coalesces short with the ō-.
omundu weKima - a Kima person/a person of Kima omundu weBunyole - a person of the Bunyore(country)
but,
omundu waBanyole - a person of the Banyore tribe

(Note: When a possessive particle does not follow a noun directly, the initial vowel to which it refers is prefixed to the possessive particle.) 16.AbEshitemi bali hoena? 17.Uno nowabandu baliia.

Kalukhasia muhuluyia:
1.Ruth's child is ill. 2.Jacob's son is well. 3.The wife of Otieno is well. 4.The wife of this man is cooking. 5.The Mwihila girl is standing over there. 6.Where are that woman's children eating? 7.Mr. Smith's workman is a local person. 8.The wife of that man yonder is eating. 9.These people's children are well. 10.The Idakho people are here. 11.This man is the husband of that woman yonder. 12.Those boys yonder are paying dowry for Kisa girls. 13.The healthy people of Kakamega are afraid of the sick people of (at) Kima. 14.The children of these women are crying. 15.Where are those boys from (lit. the ones of where)? 16.Where are the ones (relatives/children/people) of Eshitemi? 17.This one is the one of those people yonder.

Possessives With Demonstratives

In English we say, "This is my child, that is his, and those are hers." The Māluyia is more specific. He says, "the one of this one"(unu - by me and away from you; or uyu - all of us near but equidistant from each other), "the one of that one"(uyo - by you), "the one of that one yonder"(ula - some distance away from both of us). The possessive particle can be joined to any demonstrative. Symbol for possessive particle: PF; for initial vowel: IV.

The possessive particle coalesces long with ifwe= "we/us," irwe= "you," and demonstratives beginning with 2, 6, and 0.

omwans wooyo - the child of that one
omulina weewfe - our friend
abana beenywe - your (pl.) children
omwana waabo - the child of those (by you)

A w glide comes between the possessive particle and a following demonstrative which begins with u. There is no coalescence.

omwana wamuno - the child of this one
owawulia - the one of that one yonder (Note the initial vowel of the noun since the noun is absent.)
abawuyu - the ones of this one (You, "this one," and "I" are all near but equidistant from each other.)

Some dialects have the a of the possessive coalesce short with an o before the w glide and with an e before y, as, owowuno, oweyabo, etc.

Chart of Possessive-Demonstrative Combinations

IV PF. this,these this,these that,these that/those yonder
|the one of|very near,|equidistant,|relatively|far,|far from us both|
|the ones of|by me|relatively|far,|by you|
|0|wa-|unu|luvi|yvo|ula|
|2|be-|bano|yaba|yabo,abo|bala|

Note: The ula-bala forms in some dialects are ula-bala.

Either possessive particle can be prefixed to any of the above demonstratives, giving "the one/ones of this/that/that one yonder/ these/those/those yonder." These combinations follow.

owawuno = the one of this one
owawuyu = the one of this one
owawuyo = the one of that one
owooyo = the one of that one
owawulia = the one of that one
abawuno = the ones of this one
abawuyu = the ones of this one
abawuyo = the ones of that one
ubocyo = the ones of that one
abawulia = the ones of that one
ababano = the ones of these
abayaba = the ones of these
abeyabo = the ones of those
ababalia = the ones of those
ababalia = the ones of those
yonder
yonder
yonder

Some dialects have owouno, oweyabo, aboulia, abeyaba, etc., but these forms are not Standard Luyia.

Absolute Pronouns
The absolute pronouns are used for various purposes and in various combinations. They are written separately, not joined to the verb. They do not take the place of the 'subject prefix, but are in addition to it.Their uses follow.
1. Alone for clarity of thought, emphasis, and contrast:
Isie ekholanga hano.- I am working here.
Iwe oteekhanga, ne ye alimenga.- You are cooking, and she is digging.
Akhulola iwe.- He sees you (not "us," which is also -khu-).
Exercise 1
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1. Isie endi hano, iwe oli heena? 2. Inywe mulimanga, ne bo bakholanga shiina?
3. Ife khulitsanga, ne bo basietsanga. 4. Iwe otsiitsanga, ne isie esikala into.
5. Bo banyweetsanga, ne ifwe khukholanga shina? 6. Inywe mu-beetsanga abafundi, ne ifwe khubeetsanga abakholi (abatiyi). 7. Ye asiettsanga, ne bo bachinjile abasa (See p. 3). 8. Inywe mukhola bulayi, ne bo bakola bubii. 9. Isie endi omulume, ne ye nomulwe. 10. Isie endi omulina wawuno, ne ye nomulina wabano. 11. Ifwe khuritsanga omusatsa womukhasi uyu, ne inywe muriitsanga owawulia. 12. Iwe osie, ne isie endeeshe.
Exercise 2

They are drinking, and what are we doing? 6. You (pl.) are fundis, and we are workmen. 7. She is grinding, and they are carrying (have entered into the state of carrying, see p. 3) the children. 8. You (pl.) are doing well, but they are doing badly. 9. I am well, but she is ill. 10. I am the friend of this one, and she is the friend of these. 11. We are afraid of this woman's husband, but you (pl.) are afraid of the one of that one yonder. 12. You (s.) are to grind, and I am to cook.
2. Absolute pronouns with na-:
This is used as a conjunctive between clauses and usually indicates a change of subject, though it may only show a contrast. When na- is used with absolute pronouns, the initial i of isie and iwe and the final a of isie are dropped, giving nasi and nave. The a of na- coalesces long with the a of

The ni copula is used with absolute pronouns instead of the verb "to be." As usual, the i of ni drops out before another vowel. The meanings are the same as for the same persons in the verb "to be."

4. Absolute pronouns with nina-:
Nina- is used with absolute pronouns, not nende, to express (2): "and" with multiple subjects or multiple objects in a sentence.
Omukhānā ninasi khusieetṣanga. - The girl and I are grinding.
Khukhoonyange yabo ninseenywe. - We are helping those people, and you.
(b) "with" or the "with" in "have, be with."
Khutsie ninawe. - Let us go with you (or, come with me/us).
Omwana ali heena? Roda ali ninaye. - Where is the child? Roda has/is with him.
(c) "by" with the passive form of the verb (to be studied later).
The initial i of ifwe and of isie and the e of isie are elided when those words are used with nina-. The a of nina- coalesces long with ifwe and inywe. See table below.
Singular
ninasi - with me, and I/me, by me
ninawe - with you, and you, by you
ninaye - with him/her, and he/she/
Plural
nineefwe - with us, and we/us, by us
nineenye - with you, and you by you
nimabo - with them, and they/them, by them

-Nyene expresses "alone," "only," or by oneself. The absolute pronoun

in person and number may precede this combination, as, isie sienyene.

No, there is not anyone here.

Relative Construction

In Luyia there are two kinds of relative construction - the direct relative and indirect. Each kind has its own type of relative particle.

1. The Direct Relative Construction

(D R P)

The direct relative particles are cu- = who (s.), and aba- = who (pl.). They are the subject prefixes of the verb of the relative clause.

Omusaatsa, ousinjilie yaho, amwenyanga. - The man who is standing over there is smiling.

Abalimanga butinyu, banyala okhulie bulayi. - Those who work hard,

are able to eat well.

When no noun, pronoun, or demonstrative precedes, the relative particles may be translated as "the one/ones who," "he/they who," etc. The subjunctive verb stems end in a, not e in relative construction.

Mbaabo abalila. 10.Niwina ukhweetsanga? Ngwwoyo, ukhweetsanga. 11.Abandu abakholanga (abatiyanga) butinyu nibo abamonyanga bulayi. 12.Abali abalwale nibeneba? Mbaabo abalwala. 13.Nibeena abamonyanga khatsotsotso? Mbalia abamwenyanga. 14.Niwina outsia Eshisumu (Kisumu) bulaano? Isie nisie outsia bulaano. 15.Iwe niwe outeekhangha? A-a, (no) shindi nisie

Possessive Pronouns
Pattern: I V + P.P + A P
The possessive pronouns are the same as the possessive adjectives except
that the initial of the noun possessed is prefixed. Whenever the noun
does not directly precede the possessive, the initial vowel is added,
making a possessive pronoun.
While in English we say, "mine/yours/his/her/ours/their," the Muluyia
says, "the one/ones of me/you/him/her/us/them."
The long forms for 2nd and 3rd persons singular are used for possessive
pronouns: owuwo, owuve, abobo, (ababo), abebe (ababe).

-Self, -Selves as Adverbs
The root of "self"and "selves" is -ene. The initial vowel of the prefix
is omitted when it is used adverbially. The meaning of this usage seems
to express the ultimate possibility of goodness, badness, or whatever
adjective may be used.
Omundu uyu nomulayi mwene. - That person is wonderful/genuinely good.
Abansiyan yabo nabatib beene. - Those boys are simply terrible.
Words such as bulayi, bubii, butinyu, etc, which begin with bu- or obuare
followed by bwene in this type of expression.
Akholanga bulayi bwene. - He is doing tops/marvellously well.
Bayinzilanga butinyu bwene. - They are working terribly hard.
Another adverbial expression is the use of okhushila followed by khwene.
Abakhaana yabo batekhangabulayi okhushila khwene. - Those girls are
cooking extremely/marvellously well

Like
There are three ways of saying "be like, resemble, seem like:"
Patterns:
1. S P + li/beetsanga + shinga
Ali shinga samwana. - He is like/resembles his father.
2. S P + fwan/nga or S P + fwanana/nga na-/nende
Afwan/nga samwana, or Afwanananga nasemwana, or
Afwananananga nends samwana. - He resembles/seems to be
like his father
3. S P + fwan/nga + shinga
Afwananga shinga samwana. - He resembles his father.
Shinga has several variations: nga, chingana, inga. Shinga may be used
with all/moun classes, but the S P takes the moun class agreement
prefixes. See at bottom of TABLE OF CONCORDS at the back of this book.

Ni Construction
Ni Construction has many uses. More will be studied about it on pp.159-169.
Pattern ni + S P + V S The e of the subject prefixes for "I," i.e., en-, enz-, eny-, end-, is elided following ni-. The i of ni- drops out before all other vowels. The full ni- remains before all consonants. The rr...tta/tawe negative is used.
It can be used to express "and, when, if," The following are some conjugations showing ni construction with consonant and vowel stem verbs, with the li verb, and negative construction.

USES OF NI CONSTRUCTION
1. Consecutive Construction - Another way of saying "and." It is used
in narration or in relating a series of events. The first verb of the
series usually sets the tense and all other verbs are in the present
tense in ni construction. When there is a change of subject, there is
usually a transitional form if, ni construction is continued. Otherwise
the first verb following the change of subject sets the tense again.
Omukhasi ateekha nalisia elwanyi halima. - The woman cooks and
and eats and goes outside and digs.

Not Yet
This literally is expressed by the idea "is still to do a thing."
Pattern: S P + shi + li + okhu + V S. This is the most common form.
Omuteshi ashili okhuteekha. - The cook has not yet cooked (lit. He is still to cook).
Usually when a question has been asked before in which the main verb is used, the infinitive of that verb is not repeated in the answer.
Kabole witsile? Ashili. - Has Kabole come? Not yet (lit. he is still).

Forming Nouns From Verbs
All nouns are not formed in the same way. The rule is only general.

, emilango 7. omulimo, emilimo 8. omusilo, emisilo 9. omulemo, emilam-
.
Locatives
These are called prepositions in English, but in Luyia they express location
mostly, although they also are used to express time, etc.
The locatives ikulu, hasi,elwanyi (esiowa,esioba), mukeri, and haskari
are always written separately. All others join to the verb as suffixes,
or prefixes. A dash (-) written before a locative indicates that it is
a suffix; a dash written after it indicates that it is a prefix. When
locatives are prefixes, the first letter of the noun or adjective to
which it is joined drops out. This does not apply if the noun is in a
locative noun class.
Locative prefixes beginning with e-, ewa-, and ena- all have the matching
suffix -yo. The prefix ha- has the suffix -ho; khu- takes -kho;
and mu- takes -mwo.
When locatives are joined to a capitalized word, the first letter of the
word is dropped, unless the word is in a locative noun class, and the
second letter of the noun is capitalized: mu + Oluluyia = mululuyia
in Luyia, etc. If an initial vowel is needed for coalescence with the
khu- mu-, an o comes into play: Abomwihila - Mwihila people.
There is a combination of the locative e with the possessive particle
for places of distance, wa, which combine with absolute pronouns used
with the possessive adjectives, making such expressions as "our place,"
"your place," etc.
Pattern: e+ wa + A P
ewanje - my home place/at mine eweefwe - our home place/at ours
ewuwo - your home place/at yours eweenywe - your home place/at yours
ewuwe - his/her home place/at his/ ewabwe/ewabo - their home place/
at hers at theirs
This is really a noun class and has all agreements as any noun class.

Some....others
When contrasts, or comparisons are expressed, usually the first word for
"some" is milala for this class; and (e)chindi for "others." Some areas
use (e)chindi for both expressions. The e of echindi is elided when it
follows directly the noun it modifies. Where there are no comparisons or
contrasts, echindi and okundi are used. Emikyo milala nemimbichiti, ne
echindi nemirambi - Some ropes are short, and others are long. Emikunda
chindi nemikali - Some gardens are large. The same applies to (e)kundi;
mulala,...okundi - one.....the other. Omubayo mulala nomulayi, ne okundi
nomubili - One game is good, and the other one is bad; or in some areas:
Omubsyo kundi nomulayi, ne okundi nomubili.

suffixes. Frequently the causative form of the verb and the simple
form have the same meaning, as, bala - count, and basia - count. All
verbs do not have causative forms. In which cases when one wishes to
express the idea "cause to do something," one uses the verb chila -
cause, or lake/biila - command.
The causative suffixes are -isia, -ia, and -sia; sometimes -chia
which results from -ia following kh.
Ways in Which Causative Verbs Are Formed
1. An obsolete form in which very few verbs appear.
Pattern: VR + ika (if ultimate vowel of root is ā, ī, or ū).
Pattern: VR + eka (if ultimate vowel of root is ē or ō).
sma - stand still becomes emekha - erect posts for wall of
house, exalt to kingship.
bunga (obsolete) - gather together becomes bunjikha - pile up,
gather together in heap.
2. Monosyllabic verbs.
Group a:
Pattern: VS + isia (long coalescence)

, finish

CHAPTER 11
The Pronominal Concord
There are fourteen noun classes in Luyia, and each class has a basic agreement particle called the Pronominal Concord. Through this concord all the parts of the sentence are brought into agreement. It is the basis for forming demonstratives, possessives, subject-and object prefixes, numbers, relative particles, and many other things.
The person class singular and class 5 singular are irregular, and class 3 has a few irregularities. These will be explained as we come to them. The original prefix of class 5 was ini. This will account for some of the irregularities. The pronominal concord for class 1 is u.
Finding the pronominal concords.
1. Discard the initial vowel, if there is one, of the noun prefix.
2. Except for locative noun classes and person class singular, change an n or m to k. Otherwise use the consonants in the prefix.
3. Add the following vowel and you have the pronominal concord.
The following table shows the noun class numbers, the noun prefixes from which the pronominal concords are formed, and the pronominal concords for each class.
Class Number: 1 2 3 4
Class Prefix: omu - aba omu - emi (e)li - ama eshi - ebi
Pronom. Concord: u ba ku chi* li ka shi bi
Class Number: 5 6 7 8 9
Class Prefix: in(i)*-tsi olu -tsin akha - oru obu okhu
Pronom. Concord: y(i)chi tsi lu tsi kha ru bu khu
Class Number: 10 11 12 13 14
Class Prefix: (a)ha (o)khu (o)mu oku - emi e(i)n - tei(n)
Pronom. Concord: ha khu mu mu ku chi yi,chi tai
* The second i no longer appears in class five singular prefix. There are two pronominal concords for it. The chi is used as an object prefix and one of two other places, but the yi, or simply i, is used at all other times. The same is true of class 14 singular. The chi of this class and classes 2 plural and 13 plural are derived from the fact that an i follows the k which has been taken from n or m, thus changing the k to ch because of palatalization.

- 63 -
Explanations of some of the prefixes.
1. Noun and adjective prefixes.
Class 3 singular often has irregularities. The prefix li is used before noun and adjective stems beginning with consonants.
The ali prefix is used before noun and adjective stems beginning with vowels.
Following the words bulli, omwene, and abeene the entire li prefix is elided. But if ali is the prefix, only the e is elided.
The e always comes into play with ni copula, na-, possessives, likena, shika = every, or any coalescence.
Class 5 singular and plural has various prefixes for nouns and adjectives. Foreign words usually use e as the prefix for for the singular, and etsi for the plural. This has not been recognized in Luyia, but most Baluyia, even of the Central Luyia area, use them.
The prefixes for both nouns and adjectives singular are:
i-, or in- before consonant stems; in- before adjectives.
ind- before the i of stems formed from reflexive verbs;
iny- before vowel stems followed by n or m;
inz- before all other vowel stems.
The plural follows the same rules as those given above, using tsi-, tsin-, tsind-, tsiny-, and tsain- prefixed to noun stems. Adjectives do not use the i- or isi- prefixes; they take only in- and tsain- before consonants.
Class 6 plural follows the same rules for both nouns and adjectives as those for plural adjectives in Class 5, i.e., the prefixes are always tsin- before consonants, not tsi-.
Class 14 follows the same rules for adjectives as for adjectives in Class 5, both singular and plural.
The noun prefixes vary. The prefix e is a locative of place. Often it is superimposed upon another locative of place, as, ebu-, emu-, etc.
When nouns in this class have plurals, the plural prefixes are tsi-, and tsin-, agreeing with their singular counterparts.
For all nouns and adjectives in classes 5, 6, and 14 an initial e comes into play for the ni copula or for coalescence before those nouns or adjectives whose prefixes begin with i.
Classes 10, 11, and 12 are also locative classes. The vowels in parentheses are only for use with the ni copula or when one is needed for coalescence. They do not belong on the nouns themselves.
2. Subject prefixes.
With the exception of the person class, the pronominal concords (P C for patterns given), and subject prefixes are the same. The yi- P C is used for the singular subject prefixes for classes 5 and 14. The y- only is used before vowels and yi- before consonants. Since the initial vowel of a vowel-stem verb is always long in pronunciation, it is always pronounced long when the y- is prefixed to it.
Demonstratives, the -ene words for "self" and "elves," the stems -ri = thus, like this; -rio = like that, that way; and -rie = how? are all brought into agreement with a sentence noun subject by use of the pronominal concord and subject prefixes, which, with the exception of the person class, are synonymous with the pronominal concords. Charts for all these will be given here.
The stems -nji and -inji = much, many are brought into agreement by the use of adjective prefixes. A chart of these also follows.

The Person Class

The Tree Class

This has been dealt with in detail in chapters seven through ten.
The Word Class
(e)li - ama
The principal word in this class is likhuwa - word matter, affair; and amakhuwa - words, matters, affairs. These two words with their agreement particles cover a vast area of expressions, including the impersonal "it" expressions, such as, "It is necessary," etc.
Many fruits are in this class: amaramwa (amakomia) - bananas.
Liquids and masses of substance may be in it: amafura - fat, oil, etc; amatsi - water; amalwa - beer; ambebele - milk, etc.
Parts of the body which appear in pairs often take the plural of this class: eshirwi - ear may become amarwi - pair of ears, etc.
Masses of things or a large group of things may take the plural of this class: obwina - a hole becomes ameena - a group of holes as are dug for building a house; abaana - children takes amana - masses of children, etc.
Contemptuous expressions are in this class: lisataa - a good-for-no-man. Be careful in the use of this form.
Before vowels the ama- prefix coalesces long.

Forming Nouns From Verbs

Forming Nouns From Verbs

Class 5
The Animal Class
(e)i(n, nd, ny, nz) - (e)tsi(n, nd, ny, nz)
See page 63 for uses of noun and adjective prefixes for this class.
The rules of nasalization apply to nouns in this class when the prefixes are in or tsin. Ingubo - garment comes from the stem kubo, and nasalizes: in + kubo = ingubo. Sometimes when the prefix is in or tsin, and a nasal follows in the next syllable, the nasalized consonant in between is elided: bona - see - in + bon + i = imoni - eye.
The n and b have nasalized to mb, and because of the n in the following syllable, the b has dropped out. The same is true of henge-look. En + henga may = chenge. But the n may remain and n and h nasalize to mb, in which case the b usually drops out to = smenge - I look.
Vocabulary
tsiylila, khalange - fry, roast paasa - iron (garments)
tsukha - pour -nulu - fatty, greasy
imeesa - table tsimesa - tables
isahaani - plate tsishaani - plates
isabuuni - soap tsisabuni - soap, soaps
ikabati - cupboard tsikabati - cupboards
isachi - butter tsisagh - butters
ichai - tea tsichai - teas (various kinds)
ikahawa - coffee tsikahawa - coffees (varieties)
ichupa - bottle, glass jar tsichupa - bottles, glass jars
ingubo - dress, garment tsingubo - dresses, clothes
ibarwa - letter tsibarwa - letters
ibaasha - envelope tsibaasha - envelopes
isibitali - hospital tsisibitali - hospitals
ing'ombe - cow tsing'ombe - cows
inyama - meat, animal tsinyama - meats, animals
ingokho - chicken tsingokho - chickens
inzala - hunger, famine tsinzala - hunger, famines
ihawa, imbaati - axe tsihaya, tsimbaati - axes
ikanisa - church tsikanisa - churches
inzu, inyumba - house tsinzu, tsinyumba - houses
ichumbi - salt tsichumbi - salts
ipasii - an iron tsipasii - irons
inyanya - tomato tsinyanya - tomatoes
itaalo - towel tsitaalo - towels
injila - way, road, path tsinjila - ways, roads, paths
ifula - rain iyabala - drape over shoulder
- ranzayi - red (a garment)
Forming Nouns
Nouns are formed from verbs in all classes. But because of so many prefixes in this class we shall give noun stems, some from verbs; and other pure noun stems to show the use of the various prefixes.
Stem Prefixes Singular Plural Meaning
-taywa i-, tsi- itaywa tsitaywa rooster(s)
-lubi in-, tsin- indubi tsindubi small basket(s)
-haywa i(n)-tsi(n)- ihaywa tsihaywe axe(s)
-iyibela* ind-, tsind- indiyabela tsindiyabala draped garment
-ibulo inz-, tsinz- inzibulo tsinzibulo line of ancestry
-umbashe iny-, tsiny- inyumbashe tsinyumbashe building(s)
Iyabala is a reflexive verb, hence the ind- and tsind- prefixes.
Forming Adjectives
Adjectives follow the same principles as for nouns given above.
-akanyu inz-, tsinz- inzakanyu tsinzakanyu red
-imbichiti iny-, tsiny- inyimbichiti tsinyimbichiti short
-ihaanu ind-, tsind- indihaanu tsindihaanu dedicated

Class 6
The Long Class
olu - (e)tsĩn- (nd-,ny-,nz-)
See page 63 for nouns and adjectives for this class. Things which are tall or long in proportion to their diameter are often included in this class.
olukalamu - pencil; olussala - a long stick; olukulu - long mountain; olubia - railway line in contrast to eshibia - piece of iron.
The plural prefix for this class is always tsĩn- before consonants.
The olu- in this class is the concord of time. Olwa, an indirect relative particle meaning "when she time when" is taken from this class. Such expressions as olwaleelo, leelo luno - today; nolwa, nilwo olwa - it is when; and as an idiom "that is how it is" are all of this class.

Class 7
The Diminutive Class
akha - eru
Any noun may be put into this class by substituting the prefixes for this class for the regular prefixes. The same is true of adjectives.
This is called the diminutive class because it indicates that things are very small. It may be used in an offensive way, depending upon the tone of voice. Words in this class are often used to minimize things, as, Khutsĩ khulie akhalilwa. - Let us go eat a bite of food. And when one goes, a feast is served to him. This class is also used for affectionate or endearing terms, as, akhaana khanje - my little baby, my dear one. It is sometimes used for praise.

Class 8
The Abstract Noun Class
obu
A great many nouns in this class are formed from nouns, adjectives, and active and passive forms of verbs. Many are abstract nouns.
1. Nouns from Verbs.
active passive
obuleshelĩ - forgiveness (by giver) obuleshelĩ - forgiveness (received)
obwiri - murder (of murderer) obwiri - murder (of murdered)
obuhonĩa - salvation (of saviour) obuhonĩbĩ - salvation (of one saved)
2. Abstract Nouns,
obwana - childhood obuyinda - wealth, riches
obulwale - illness obuchesi - wisdom,intelligence
These are formed from nouns, adjectives, and verbs.
3. Collective Nouns,
obwba + mushrooms obunyasi - grass, lawn
obwya - hairs of animal skin obule - dwarf millet
These verbs are all plural. When a singular form is needed, the plu- prefix is used, as, olwoba - a mushroom; olunyasi - blade of grass.
4. Substances.
obusela - gruel obongo - brain
obusuma - stiff gruel obusi - reel of cotton, thread
obuushi - honey (olusi - a piece of thread)
5. Singular Nouns,
A very few words in this class are singular in form, and when a plural is desired, the noun goes into the ama- class. This plural form often denotes great masses.
obubukha - sugar ants = amabukha - masses of sugar ants.
obwina, obuko - a hole = ameena, amako - many holes

POSSessive PARTICles WITH DEMONSTRATIVE PRONouns
These were given with the first two noun classes on pages 11 and 45. The same principles apply throughout all classes. More than two thousand combinations can be made from the chart below by prefixing the possessive particles in the left column to each of the demonstratives in the other columns. If no noun precedes immediately, the initial vowel is prefixed to the possessive particle. The initial vowels are given in parentheses in the chart below. The possessive particles coalesce long with those demonstratives beginning with vowels.
Pattern: (IV) + FP + Demonstrative - elikuno

The plural of class 14 is the same as the plural of class 5. Some dialects coalesce the possessive particle with an initial s before those demonstratives beginning with ya- or yi-, and with the initial vowel of those ending with -no. In such cases the pronunciation should be as in those dialect areas, but Standard Luyia is written with only the possessive a before all these: abayabo - the ones of those, may be pronounced abeyabo; gilakuno - the one of this one, may be pronounced as gilakuno.

Ordinal Numbers
Every ordinal number has a possessive particle prefixed to it. The possessive particle agrees in class and number with the noun or pronoun antecedent. If no noun immediately precedes, the initial vowel is prefixed to the possessive particle. There are various patterns.
1. First. Pattern: (IV) + PP + mbeli/okhuranga (short coalescence) elambeli - the first one (class 3); eyokhurange - the first one
2. Second through sixth. Pattern: (IV) + PP + kha + NoS eshiakhabili - the second one (class 4); olwekhassasabe - the sixth
3. Seventh through tenth. Pattern: (IV) + PP + NoS obuko bwamunaane - the eighth hole; abikombe bielikhumi - the tenth cups. (e of class 3 comes into play for short coalescence)
4. Tenth and multiples. Pattern: (IV) + PP + 10 or multiple eshichiiko shielikhumi - the tenth spoon ing'ombe yamakhumi kabili - the twentieth cow
5. All firsts above tens. Pattern: (IV) + PP + 10 or multiple + na + lulala ovelikhumi nalulele - the eleventh one (person) imusi yamakhumi kabili nalulela - the twenty-first goat
6. All seconds through sixths above the tens. Pattern: (IV) + PP + 10 or multiple + na + kha + NoS ovamakhumi kataru nakhabild - the thirty-second one (class 1) elielikhumi nakhane - the fourteenth one (class 3)

Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.Do you see this cat? Yes, I see it. 2.Have you just chopped off the banana leaves? Yes, I have just chopped them off. 3.How do you count the days of one week? I count them like this: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. 4.Where is the saucepan? Anzemo is washing it outside. 5.The father wants to buy shoes for his boy. Where can he get them? 6.This book is good. Do you want to read it? 7.Pick the flowers now. I am picking them. 8.Is the owner of the banana patch chopping off leaves in it today? Yes, he is chopping them off in it. 9.Fry the meat. I just now fried it. 10.Tell Sarah to set the table. Oh! she has just finished setting it. 11.Arthur, herd the cow. I am herding it. 12.Sing (pl.) this song. We have just sung it. 13.Grandmother is telling stories. Do you hear them? Yes, I hear them. 14. Are you doing arithmetic now? Yes, I am doing it now. 15.Is the sheep nursing the lamb? Yes, it is nursing it. 16.Sweep the tiny rooms. I am sweeping them. 17.Do you see the face of that goat? Yes, I see it. 18.Look how that giant yonder is carrying the huge club! My goodness! He is carrying it on his head.
Near Past Tense of Verbs
This tense is used for anything which has happened today only. For this time span there is the simple past and the present perfect tense. With the exception of the subject prefix for the 3rd person singular the difference is a matter of tone. The subject prefix for the 3rd person singular in the present perfect tense is u before consonants and w before vowels. Otherwise all subject prefixes for this tense are type A, the same as for the present tense.

With the exception of the 3rd person singular there is no way in
writing to show the difference between the simple past and the present
perfect tense in the Near Past time span. The real difference is
one of tone. There is a range of five tones for verbs in this tense;
high, medium-high, medium, medium-low, and low. For representing
these tones the following chart can be a guide:

A dash represents the medium tone:
A dot one space above represents a medium-high tone:
A dot two spaces above represents a high tone:
A dot one space below represents a medium-low tone:
A dot two spaces below represents a low tone:

In the simple present stem of the monosyllabic verbs there are four
which are spoken on a lower tone than the others. These four follow
a different tone-pattern than the others in the simple past, but all
follow the same tone-pattern in the present perfect tense form. The
following tone-patterns with the verbs in their proper classifications
are shown in the chart given below.

Tone-Patterns for Monosyllabic Verbs in the Near Past
| Infinitive | Simple Past | Present Perfect |
|------------|-------------|----------------|
| okhushia   | bushieele   | bushieele       |
| okhube     | abeelee     | ubeelee         |
| okhura     | areelee     | ureelee         |
| okhua      | aheelee     | uheelee         |

Note that all present perfect tense tones are on a lower tone-pattern

The simple past translated into English is of course: I ate, you ate, he/she ate, we ate, you ate, they ate, it ate, they ate, etc. The present perfect form is: I have eaten, you have eaten, he/she has eaten, we have eaten, you have eaten, they have eaten, it has eaten. All verbs do not fit completely into these two forms exactly as they do in English. But this true of all languages; no one form is the exact equivalent in every way to any other one form in another language.

Exercise 31
Kalukhasis muLusungu:
1.Abacheni babeelohelo leelo. 2.Amatsti kali heena? Kabeeloh hamo mu-kamba kuno. 3.Nyina uheele omwana amatsi anywe. 4.Amatsti kahweele. 5.Mbeela abasaana omukate. 0! kwosi kuhweele. 6.Oreels heema omubano? Engureele hano. 7.Abakhanaa basie amatuuma bulsano. Basieele mukamba kuno. 8.Kukhu afwile mushilo (mubutukhu), ne bulsano omulwale uno yeenya okhufwa. 9.Amakanda kailiwe nende abasaana kosi pe. 10.Ebikombe bireelwe mukabsti. 11.Tsing'ombe tsitsile heena? Tsitsile okhwaya. 12.Amatsti kayiile. 13.Amatsti kayiile bulayi mukamba kuno. 14.Bushieele. 15.Bushieele bwangu mukamba kuno. 16.Umanyie abakholi nibatsille.

Exercise 32
Kalukhasis muLuluyisa:
1.The guests were here today. 2.Where is the water? It was here this morning. 3.The mother has given the child some water to drink (that he may drink). 4.The water is gone (has come to an end). 5.Give the child some bread for me. Oh, it is all gone (it has all come to an end). 6.Where did you put the knife? I put it here. 7.The girls may grind the maize now. They ground it this morning. 8.Grandmother died in the night, and now this sick person is about to die. 9.The beans have all been eaten by the children. 10.The cups have been put in the cupboard. 11.Where have the cows gone? They have gone to graze. 12.The water is hot (has become hot). 13.The water got hot well this morning. 14.Good morning (it has become light). 15.It got light quickly this morning. 16.Let me know when the workmen have gone.

2. Verbs ending in -ia.
Active.
Pattern:VR + ye/yenje
kasi + ye = kasiye. Engasiye ingubo. - I fixed the dress.
osi + yenje = osiyenje. Yoosiyenje ebikombe. - She has been washing the cups.

Passive.
Pattern: VR + ibwe/ibungwe
kusi + ibwe = kusibwe. Amakanda kakusibwe. - The beans were sold.
kosi + ibungwe = kosiibungwe. Amapesa kakosiibungwe. - The money has been being lost.

In the simple past the polysyllabic verbs ending in -ia seem to follow one general pattern of tone: medium, high, medium, low. The tone patterns of the dissyllabic verbs vary according to the pitch in the present tense stem. A table of some of the verbs and their tone patterns for infinitives and past tenses follow.

Absolute Pronouns
We have used the absolute pronouns for the person class very much. Their formation is irregular. But all other absolute pronouns follow a regular pattern of formation.
Pattern: PC + o
Ku + o = kwo; ku + o = kwo, etc.
All pronominal concords ending in a coalesce short with the o.
ba + o = bo; ka + o = ko; kha + o = kho; ha + o = ho.
Besides being used alone to express contrast or clarity of though, there are six combinations of absolute pronouns. We shall study five of these combinations in this chapter, and the sixth, which is the use of the possessive particle with absolute pronouns to form possessive adjectives and possessive pronouns, will be studied in the next chapter. The following tables show the absolute pronouns for all classes with five combinations.

Relative Construction in the Intermediate Past Tense
1.Consonant stems, direct relative.
Positive. Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + same endings as near past
Negative. Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + VR + same endings as near past tense
2.Vowel stems, direct relative.
Positive. Pattern: Type B DRP + ya + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + ya + VR + near past endings
3.Consonant stems, indirect relative.
Positive. Pattern: IRP + Type B SP + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + raa + VR + near past endings
4.Vowel stems, indirect relative.
Positive. Pattern: IRP + Type B SP + ya + VR + near past endings
Negative. Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + raa + ya + VR + near past endings

Possessive Adjectives and Pronouns
See pages 30 and 57 for a revision of possessive adjectives and pronouns
. They are a combination of initial vowels, possessive particles,
and absolute pronouns,
1.Possessive adjectives.
a.second and third persons singular, always short coalescence.
(1) shortened suffix form.
Pattern: PP + u (2nd person) -woi:-boi:-kwoi:-chio, etc.
Pattern: PP + e (3rd person) -wei:-kwe:-chie:-be, etc.
(2) long form; stands alone.
Pattern: PC + PP + o ( kukwo;chichio, etc.
Exception: The person class prefixes a w- before PC + wuwo.
Pattern: PC + PP + e (3rd person) uuwe;kukwe;chichie.
pronominal concords ending in a:
Pattern: PP + o/e + PP + o/e babo,bebe;koko,keke, etc.
Some dialects hold to the patterns under (2) above, as,
baboo;kakoo;khakho hahoo;babe;kake;khakhe;hahe.
b.all other persons and classes.
Pattern: PP + AP
Table for Forming Possessive Adjectives and Possessive Pronouns
The pronominal concords are given in parentheses for use with
the 2nd and 3rd persons singular of the person class when forming
the long forms: kukwo;chichie;okukwo;echichie, etc.

For Past Tense of Verbs
1.Consonant stem verbs. (from fifth day on back indefinitely)
Simple past and present perfect tenses:
Pattern: Type B SF + VR + a
Ndatsia. - I went. Batsia. - They have gone.
The tone for the simple past is relatively low on the subject prefix. The tone for the present perfect is high on the subject prefix. This is true for both consonant and vowel stem verbs.
2.Vowel stem verbs.
a.simple past:
Pattern: Type B SF + VR + a (long coalescence)
Khweetsa. - We came. Beeka bulayi. - They studied well.
b.present perfect:
Pattern: Type B SF + ya + VR + a (long coalescence)
Khwayeska butinyu. - We have studied hard.
Object prefix "me" for immediate past and far past present perfect tense is yan.
Conjugations
Simple Past (Consonant) Present Perfect
Singular Plural Singular Plural
ndatsia khwatsia ndatsia khwatsia
watsia mwatsia watsia mwatsia
yatsia batsia yatsia batsia
(vowel)
ndeebaala khweebaala ndyeebaala khweebaala
weebaala mweebaala weyeebaala mweebaala
yeebaala beebaala wayeebaala bayeebaala
The continuous endings are the same as for those for the various types of verbs in the present tense. However, the meaning is usually "used to do." The far past continuous ending for the verb "to be" is -nji. Yalini omwechesia. - He used to be a teacher. To indicate that a thing was in the process of being done, a compound form is used. This will be studied later.
Simple Far Past with Consonant Stems

Relative Construction in the Far Past Tense
There seem to be no differences of tone or form to differentiate between the simple past and the present perfect tenses within this far past time span.in relative construction.
1.Consonant stems (or with a following prefix which begins with a consonant).
Positive construction (direct relative):
Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Omundu owatsia ngwuwuno. - Here is the person who went.
Negative construction:
Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta/tawe
Ouraatsia ta, ngwooyo. - There is the one who did not go.
(indirect relative)
Positive construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type B SP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Omwana, owa omukhaana valola, ailanga. - The child whom the girl saw is crying.
Negative construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type A SP + raa + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta/tawe
Omwana, owa omukhaana arealola ta,bulaand ngwowulia. - The child whom the girl did not see is now over yonder.
2.Vowel stems.
Positive construction. (direct relative):
Pattern: Type B DRP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga (long coalescence)
Omusaala okwaama ebiamo ebinji ngwokuno. - The tree which has borne much fruit is this one.
Negative construction:
Pattern: Type A DRP + raa + ya + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga + ta
Omusaala okuraasyama ebiamo ebinji ta ngwokwo. - There is the tree which did not bear much fruit.
(indirect relative)
Positive construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type B SP + VR + a/ange/njia/itsanga
Abeechi, aba omwechesia veechesia, nabachesi. - The pupils whom the teacher taught are clever.
Negative construction:
Pattern: IRP + (subject) + Type A SP + raa + ya + VR + a + ta
Abaana, aba khurasyosia ta, bali abamali. - The children whom we did not wash were dirty.

Emphasis
There many means for adding emphasis to Luyia expressions.
1.Pattern: PC + ene (as an adverbial superlative expression)
Omutoka nomulayi kwene. - The car is simply grand.
2.By using okhushila, muno, okhushila muno, or munonono.
Akholanga bulayi okhushila. - He is doing exceedingly well.

Augmentative Verbs
This derived form is formed in the same way as the Reversive. But
the meanings of these verbs are an augmentation of the meaning of
the original verb. The meanings of the various forms will make it
clear to the student whether the verbs are reversive or augmentative.
All verbs do not appear in all forms. In fact, no one verb appears in
all the derived forms. If a verb is in the reversive, it cannot
be in the augmentative, and vice versa.
1.Verbs whose ultimate vowel of the root is a, e, i, or u.
Pattern:VR + ula/ulula/ula
ching + ula = chinguala - raise, lift up.
In the ula suffix the first l of the ulula seems to have dropped
out leaving ula.
2.Verbs whose ultimate vowel of the root is o.
Pattern: VR + ola/ola/ola
lond + oola = londoola - follow along a path or trail.
Again it seems that the ola is the ola ending with the first l
elided.

Relative Construction in the "Li" Future
1.Direct relative.
Positive.
Pattern: Type A DRP + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Oullitsia niwing? - Who is it who will go?
Negative.
Pattern: Type A DRP + ra + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga + ta/taw
Abaralitsia ta - They who will not go.
2.Indirect relative.
Positive.
Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + li + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Omundu, owa alilola - The person whom he will see.
Negative.
Pattern: IRP + Type A SP + ra + li + VR + a/anga, etc. + ta/taw
Gmutoka,okwa aralilola ta - The car which he will not see.

Ideophones
Ideophones are a separate part of speech in Luyia. Their function is similar to that of an adverb. They seek to imitate the sound of the idea which a word represents. They add meaning to verbs, adjectives, nouns, etc. They may be monosyllabic, disyllabic, or polysyllabic, and have definite tone patterns. Many are used only with specific words. The first two in the list below can be used with many kinds of words, while the others are more limited.
Matching words Ideophones Sentences
many used po - much, very Nobubbi po. - It is very bad.
many used pe - all Amokonda Rahucole pe. - The beans are all gone.

Extensive Verbs
These verbs indicate an extended or repeated action, at times. At other times they are used in a polite sense, as, "please do so-and-so." Again, depending on the tone of voice, they may be used to express exasperation: Well, go ahead and do it then.
Mbeelaka. - Please excuse me; or, Mbeelaka. - Well, just go ahead and put up with me!
Voice intonation makes the difference.
1.Monsyllabic verbs.
Pattern: VS + itsaka (coalescing group a)
Nyweetsaka. - Please drink.
Pattern: VR + itsaka (non-coalescing group b)
Liitsaka. - Please go ahead and eat.
2.Verbs (not monosyllabic) ending in -ia.
Pattern: VR + chie
Kasichie ingubu. - Please fix the dress.
3.All other verbs.
Pattern: VS + ka
4.When verb stems end in -e, as subjunctive mood or imperative plural
a.monsyllabic use itseche
b.other verbs ending in -ia follow Pattern: VR + chie
c.all other verbs follow Pattern: VR + e + che

nala (ng'aya) - become accustomed/ adjusted to, be usual/customary
shinda,cheleva (cheleba) - be late, tarry
laama - bequeath, beseech, pray
obulaame - inheritance
omukhalachi - judge
omusikari - policeman,soldier
omweha - bride
isindu - quail
tsilila - get wet
yabila - bury
chelela - return (home)
Evana - term of respect to a man; abaakukas - ancestors, grand-fathers
eshilindwa - grave
eshilifu - chest
ebweneyo - right there.
Conditional Clause "If"
The ni construction which we studied in Chapter 6 could be interpreted as "if," "when," or "and." There is a reduplicated form of ni construction which means only "if."
Pattern: ni + SP + ba + ni + SP + VS (positive)
Pattern: ni + SP + ba + ni + SP + ra + VS + ta (negative)
Conjugations
tsia
Singular
1st per. nimba ninzia - if I go
2nd per. noba notsia - if you go
3rd per. naba natsia - if he/she goes
Plural
nikhuba nikutsia - if we go
nimuba nimutsia - if you go
nibabs nibatsitsanga - if they are going (new or always)
nikuba nikutsia - if it goes etc.
tsia
1st per. nimba ninzitsa - if I come nikhuba nikritsa - if we come
2nd per. noba niwitsa - if you come nimuba nimitsa - if you come
3rd per. naba nyeetsa - if he/she nibaba nibetsa - if they come etc.
The second form in this "if" clause can be in the present tense as given above: nibaba nibatsia - if they go.
Or it may be in a past tense: nibaba nibatsiile - if they have gone.
Or it may be in a future tense:nibaba nibatsie - if they shall go.
The main clause may express many things: commands, both imperative and subjunctive; clauses using enya, nyala, etc. followed by infinitives or subjunctive forms; wishes, instructions, desires, permissions, etc. in the subjunctive mood; or a statement in a future tense.
Exercise 1
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Noba nomulola, mubolele yeetsa. 2.Nimube nimutsia Nairobi, munderele ingubo imbia. 3.Nimba ninyoole eshitabo yishio, enyenya okhushisoome. 4.Nibaba naekhole bulayi mumareebu, nababire mumukanda kwakhataru. 5.Omutoka nikuba nakukasibwe mukamba, khwakhatsie Nakuru teinyanga taine nitsihwele. 6.Noba niwenya, onyala okhunaba bulayi. 7.Tsing'ombe tsino-tsibili nitsiba hitsikhomele, khulitsisiza mu-shiselelo. 8.Omwayi naba narayanga tsimbusi bulayi, shitsilikhomela bulayi tawe. 9.Nimba nimulola, nemubolele okhvitse okhukhaaonya. 10.Petero naba nalio, yeembe olwimbo bulaso. 11.Ifule niyiba niyitsa lichuuma lino, nakhura sche omukunda. 12.Ebiano nibibe nibienjile, khwakhabinochche Okwakhabili.

4.If they succeed (do well) in the examinations, they will pass into the third class. 5.If the car will be fixed tomorrow, we shall go to Nakuru four days hence. 6.If you (s.) want to, you are able to sew well. 7.If these two cows are fat, we shall kill them for the wedding (during the wedding). 8.If the shepherd does not herd the goats well, they will not fatten well. 9.If I see her, I will tell her to come to visit you (s.). 10.If Peter is here, he may sing now. 11.If the rain comes this week, we shall plant the garden. 12.If the fruit is ripe (has ripened), we shall pick it Tuesday.
Contingent Mood
1.The Possible Contingent.
This mood uses the "if" clause as has been studied above, while the main, or contingent, clause verb is in the immediate past tense, and represents the idea of "would," "could," and, with haundi it is interpreted as "might." It is practically the equivalent of the English past subjunctive mood, expressing the possibility of a thing happening in the future: If he came, I would tell him, etc.
Pattern: If clause + Type B SP + kha + VR + a/anga/njia/itsanga
Naba nateekha, ndakhalia. - If she cooked, I would eat.
Notice that the "if" clause does not change in tense as it does for this type of sentence in English. Actually, the Muluyia says, "If she cooks, I would eat." But this is not idiomatic English to interpret it so.
The main clause uses the shi....tawe negative.
For expressing "might, might possibly:"
Pattern: If clause + haundi + Type B SP + kha + VR + a/anga,etc.
Haundi bakhatsia Nairobi. - They might possibly go to Nairobi
a.Expressing possibility:
Exercise 3
Kalukhasia muLusunga:
1.Bwana natsie Eshisumu mukamba? Haundi yakhatsis. 2.Abacheni na-beetse leelo? Haundi bakheetss. 3.Ing'ombe nayisi-nzwe leelo? Fwaha (haundi) yakhasinzwa. 4.Namuchielele ingo leelo? Haundi khwakhachelela (or in the indicative mood, Haundi nakhuche-lele - Perhaps we shall return). 5.Olanaba ingubo bulaano? Haundi ndakhanaaba. 6.Eshilindwa nashiyabwe leelo, noho? Haundi shiakha-yawa bulaano, shichila leelo abandu beenya okhuyabile oufwile.
Exercise 4
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.Will Bwana go to Kisumu tomorrow? He might possibly go. 2.Will the guests come today? They might come. 3.Will the cow be slaughtered today? Perhaps it might be slaughtered. 4.Will you return home today? We might return. 5.Will you sew the dress now? I might possibly sew (it). 6.Will the grave be dug today? It might be dug now, because today the people want to bury the dead person.
b."If" clauses with the contingent clauses:
There are some variations which are often used in the "if" clause in the contingent mood. Here are some.
Nimba ninzia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I went now, I would see him.
Nimba nindakhatsia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I should go now, I would see him.
Ninzia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I went now, I would see him.
Ndakhatsia bulaano, ndakhamulola. - If I should go now, I would see him.
Noba noratsia mukamba, shiwakhanyoola amakenda ta. - If you did not go tomorrow, you would not get the beans.
Noba norakhatsia mukamba, shiwakhanyoola amakenda ta. - If you should not go tomorrow, you would not get the beans.

falling.
(2)past tenses:
Pattern: SP + "to be",in past tense + ni + Type A SP + enya +
infinite
Yakhaba/abeele/yabeele/yali niyeenya okhutsia. - He was just
on the verge of going/about to go.
(3)future tenses:
Pattern: SP + "to be" in future tense + ni + Type A SP + enya
+ infinitive
Alaba/nabe/yakhabe/aliba niyeenya okhutsia. - He will be about
to go/just on the verge of going
Exercise 31
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Olwa khulileyo, abandu babeelie ahambi okhutsia. 2.Olwa omusakanula
yeetsa yino, yali ahambi okhukwe khulwe okhuchonge. 3.Olwa abakana
bamalile okhulima, abandu babeelie ahambi okhuchake. 4.Olwa khubeele
nikhwenya okhutsia okhukona, omundu yeetsile. 5.Olwa abanna babeele
nibeenya okhuchaka okhubaya, abanyina babalanjile. 6.Olwa omulilo
kwali shambi (kwali nikwenya) okhusima, omukhaana yarakhwo tsikwi
tsindi. 7.Nikhulileyo nakhunyooole mbu nababe ahambi okhulia. (or, nababe
nibeenya okhulia). 8.Ebitabu bino nibimalile okhwechelwamo nabeechi
, bishkabe nibili ahambi okhukofula. 9.Omwezi okwitwa nikuchaka
, amatsi keshitano shiserve kaliba nikali ahambi okhuhwa.
Exercise 32
Kalukhasia muLaluya:
1.When we arrived there, the people were about to go. 2.When the old
man came here, he was about to fall because of tiredness. 3.When the
girls finished digging, the others were about to begin. 4.When we
were just on the verge of going to bed (to sleep), the man came. 5.
When the children were just ready to begin playing, their mothers
called them. 6.When the fire was about to go out, the girl put more
firewood on it. 7.When we arrive there we shall find that they will
be about to eat. 8.After these books have been studied (in) by the
pupils, they will be nearly worn out. 9.At the beginning of next
month the water of our spring will nearly be gone.
c.Another form of "about to" is used if something happens to prevent
one from doing what he was about to do.
Pattern: SP + VS of "to be" in past or future tense + Type A SP +
subjunctive VS
Khubeele khulie olwa bakhulanjile okhutsia ninabo. - We were
just about to eat when they called us to go with them.
Nyinamwana yabeele atsie Mombasa, ne omwanawe yalwallile. - The
mother was just about to go to Mombasa, but her child became ill.
Shikhunya la okhulima bulaano ta.Nakhube khuchache, ne mama nakullanje
okhulia. - We cannot dig now. We shall be just about to
begin, and mother will call us to eat.

Vocabulary
fuba - spoil (by not going on to completion, as food spoiled in
cooking because the fire has gone out)
longa - make; fashion or mold with the hands
-shiamu - crooked
omukhulundu - elder, mature person, adult
Denominative Verbs
These are verbs which are derived from substantive nouns, adjectives,
and adverbs. With only an occasional exception, they are formed by
adding -kha,-ha,-ia, or -hala to the noun or adjective stem, or to
adverb. The overall idea is "to become" a certain way.
1.Those formed with -kha.
Word Stem
-lunjji - straight,righteous
kololi - straight forward, up-
-lamu - well,healthy,alive
eshimuli - flower,blossom
-lalu - mad, insane
Derived Form
lunjikha - straighten up/out,become
straight
kololokha - become straight/correct
/right
lamukha - revive,come to life
mulikha - bloom,blossom
lalukha - go mad/insane
2.Those formed with -ha.
-ochi - sharp
-imbichiti - short
-cheni - strange,new, visitor
-khongo - great, important,big
-chesi - wise,intelligent,clever
Derived Form
ochiha - become sharp
imbiha - shrink,become shorter
cheniha - visit,stay while
khongoha - become great,big,etc.
chesiha (chetsiha) - become wise/
clever
-tiiti - small, little
-inji - much, many
-rambi - tall, long
-kali - large, big, great
-khungu - old
-omwami - chief, chief person
Derived Form
tiitha - become small/little
injhe - multiply,become many
rambiha - become tall/long
kaliha - become large/big/great
khunguha - become old (people)
amilha - hold ruling position,reign
3.Those formed with -la.
-tofu - weak,lazy,lacking in determination
-bofu - blind
-kofu - old,mature,worn out
kuukhu - grandmother
Derived Form
tofula - become weak/lazy/lacking
in determination
bofula - become/go blind
kofula - become old/mature/worn
kuukhula - become/act slow like
an old woman
4.Those formed from -hala.
omukumba - a barren woman
-chesi - wise,clever,intelligent
-kara - lazy
omuyinda - rich/wealthy person
-nyelele - narrow,slender,fine
Derived Form
kumbahala - become barren
chesihala - become wise/clever
karahala - become lazy
yindihala - become rich/wealthy
nyelehala - become slender/thin;
shrink as a withered arm/leg
Many of these derived verbs can be put in the causative and other
forms: lunjisia - straighten; lamusia - revive,bring to life; injivia
- multiply (tr.), cause to increase.

10.Omundu nali nemiandu eminji, ayindhaale. 11.Tsinyanga tsino amache

Exercise 4
Kalukhasia muLuluyia:
1.That boy barely got his hands wet washing them this morning. 2.The
children hopped about for joy. 3.That person yonder marries one woman,
lives with her awhile, then sends her away and marries another one, over and over. 4.That boy reads every book he can get. 5.
I only glanced at the letter; I did not read it thoroughly. 6.A woman
gets up and lies down again and again when she is in labour. 7.Cain
was made to leave his country, and he went and wandered about in the
whole earth. 8.Where are you going? I am just taking a walk. 9.This
child is naughty; he hacks up everything he sees. 10.This tree blooms
profusely every year.
Summary of "And"
1. nina- is used for "and" before an absolute pronoun in multiple
subjects and objects in a sentence.
iwe ninaye muli abasaana butswa. - You and he are only children.
Endutsi inywe ninabo bosi. - I saw you and them also.
Omusiani ninabo batsiltsanga ingo. - The boy and they are going
home.
2. a.na- joins nouns, and all but the last in a series of nouns.
omwanu nomukheana nomukhasi nende omussatsa. - a child and a girl
and a woman and a man.
b.As a conjunctive between clauses, denoting change of subject.
Abakhana bakhoonyanga omushiele, naye alimanga. - The girls are
helping the old woman, and she is digging.
Iwe olitiitsanga, nasi endeekhanga. - You are eating and I am cookNote
that na- in this usage is with absolute pronouns.
ing.
c.As a conjunctive between infinitives indicating a sequence of acts.
Omukhasi msietsanga, nokhufuka obusuma, nokhussia mamuchele,henokhulisisa
abama. - The girl grinds and makes obusuma, and goes
for water and feeds the children.
3. nende is used in joining two nouns used as multiple subjects or
objects in a sentence, also before the last noun or infinitive in a
series.
Omukhasi nende omussatsa balimanga. - The woman and man are digging
.
Omukhasi nomukheana nende omussatsa balimanga. - The woman and
girl and man are digging.
Yeenya okhufuka nende okhulia. - She wants to make obusuma and
eat.
4. khandi a.joins two or more adjectives describing the same noun or
pronoun.
Yohana nomurambi khandi nomunyelele. - John is tall and slender.
Oli omusiro khandi omwimbichiti. - You are fat and short.
b.for joining two or more adverbs describing the same verb.
Yee lukhanga bwangu khandi butinyu. - He is running fast and hard.
c.joining two or more independent clauses having no time sequence
referring to the same subject.
Omundu uno ayinzilanga bulayi, khandi ayinzilange bwangu. - This
man works well, and he works fast.
d.joining two or more independent clauses of no time sequence which
refer to two or more subjects doing the same thing, or being the
same way.
Abakhana balimanga, khandi abasiani balimenge leelo. - The girls
are digging, and the boys are digging today.
5. ni-, or consecutive construction. See page 161. This seems to be
used when a sequence of events are related.
Mana natsia niyeelukha nalanga abandu nababoolela. - Then he went
running and called the people and told them.
6. ne as a conjunctive between a dependent and independent clause,or
those having time sequence. It is also used for "but."

More Uses of "kha"
This is a form which adds verbosity to one's speech, making it more
informal, sometimes playful, sometimes taking from the bluntness of
straightforward speech.
1. Commands.
Pattern: kha + subjunctive stem (for both singular and plural)
Khatsie. - Just go along, go ahead.
2. With tenses.
Pattern: SP + kha + VS in desired tense
Kakhali karie? - What's the matter here? or, Just what is wrong?
Exercise 5
Kalukhasia muLusungu:
1.Ekhenya okhuboola likhuwa, Khaboole. 2.Khukhatsia bulasano, noho?
Khatsie. 3.Notsie Nairobi, nokhakaluše bwangu. 4.Sing'ombe tsikhanyeеле
amatesi, nohomba tsishili? 5.Omusaala kulia kukhakhlunga
kurie? 6.Eshimeeme shielikondi shikharfwele moushina? 7.Ambeele kakhaweele
bwangu leele mbushina? 8.Okhalli namakhuwa shina? 9.Okhatekhe
shina? 10.Mukhahenganga shina?
Exercise 6
Kalukhasia muDuluyia:
1.I would just like to say a word. Go ahead and say it. 2.Shall we
just go now? Go ahead. 3.If you go to Nairobi, you will just come
straight back. 4.Now have the cows drunk water, or not yet? 5.That
tree yonder, just how is it growing? 6.Just why did the lamb die?
7.Why ever was the milk finished so quickly today? 8.Now what affares
de you (s.)-happen to have? 9.Just what are you (s.) cooking?
10.Whatever are you (pl.) looking at.
Both
There is a term which varies from one dialect to another, but which
in some means "both," or "they are included." This is the use of
ali...ali; Abana balihe, ali abasiani, ali abakhama. The children
were there, both boys and girls. Some dialects use hali...hali;
others ari...ari; and still others khali...khali.
Another way of saying "both," meaning two is:
Pattern: plural AP + mbi
bombi, chiombi, kombi, biombi, tsionambi, rwombi, etc.
Pattern: plural AP + si + plural NOP + bili
bosi babili, chiosi chibili, kosi kabilii, biosi bibili, tsiosi
tsibili, rwosi rubili, etc.
Shortened Forms and Contractions
1. Interrogatives heena? shina? wina? beena? mbushina? liina? become
: he? shi? wi? be? mbushii? lii? etc.
Ali he? - Where is she? Okholanga shi? - What are you doing?
Uyo niwi? - Who is that person? Bano nibe? - Who are these?
Notsie li? - When will you go? Okhola orio mbushi? - Why do
you do like that?
2. "If" clause.
The 1 is omitted from the ni. In some dialects the remaining n
follows the rules of nasalization, in others the n is almost inaudibly
spoken in the throat.
nibaba nbatsia = mbaba mbatsia, or nbaba nbatsia.
nikuba nkuli = ngube nguli, or nkuba nkuli.
nitsiba nitsili = nziba nzili, or, ntsiba ntsili.
nishiba nishili = nshiba nshili
nibibe nibili = mbiba mbili, or nbiba nbili.
The second forms are found in the Central Duyua area among
others.
